venues.d: The city's grande dame since 1876 — the address every other Bangkok hotel is measured against.
An Art Deco riverside retreat of just 39 suites and pool villas — a private-collector's house, not a hotel.
The house the world voted its very best — a low, garden-wrapped sanctuary on the river's quiet bend.

venues.n: Four Seasons Hotel Bangkok at Chao Phraya River
venues.d: Tiered lawns stepping down to the water, and the surest service in the city.
A W-shaped tower built to give every room the river — and a fleet of green Peninsula boats at the jetty.
Aman's return to Thailand — a hushed tower rising from century-old parkland in the heart of town.
Two hands clasped in the wai, rendered as a tower — vertical, arty and quietly grand.
Lotus ponds, teak and brick pavilions — a low-rise pocket of old Siam in the business district.
Japanese precision poured into a Bangkok tower, with a cantilevered 25th-floor pool over the city.
A tailored city house set atop the Central Embassy mall — refined, discreet, effortlessly connected.
The Ritz-Carlton's Bangkok debut inside the pixelated MahaNakhon tower — high, sleek and central.
Art Deco New York glamour in a lotus-inspired tower, above the Ratchaprasong shopping heart.
Butler service and racecourse views on Ratchadamri, connected straight to the BTS.
Hand-painted murals, a lush pool courtyard and old-Bangkok grace off the busiest corner in town.
A playful, design-forward tower on a leafy lane beside Lumphini Park.
The reborn golden-spire landmark — a homegrown grande dame, rebuilt for a new century.
Understated urban minimalism and the wellness rigour COMO is known for.
A dependable, well-run city tower plugged directly into Bangkok's shopping arteries.
An all-suite colonial-teak homage, with a vertigo-edge rooftop pool over Sukhumvit.
A discreet all-suite address with kitchens — an apartment's ease with a hotel's polish.
A colour-splashed design tower overlooking the green of Lumphini Park.
The first Thai restaurant in the world to hold three Michelin stars — Southern Thai cooking raised to the summit.
Progressive Indian theatre from Gaggan Anand — five times crowned the best restaurant in Asia.
Twin German brothers reimagining the food of their childhood, in a garden villa.
Chef Ton's love letter to his grandmother's cooking, with Wat Pho glowing through the window.
Chef Pam's Thai-Chinese story told across five floors of her family's old medicine shophouse.
The kitchen that launched Bangkok's modern-Thai movement, still setting the pace.
A home turned restaurant, cooking Thai food with a farm's rhythm and a family's warmth.
Refined French dining 61 floors up, where the whole city drops away beneath you.
A sky-high room marrying French and Japanese technique on the 65th floor.
Royal-Thai cooking staged with ceremony — the old recipes, kept alive and exact.
Chef Garima Arora's fearless, ingredient-led cooking — the first Indian woman to win a Michelin star.
The Mirazur master's Riviera seafood, brought to the Chao Phraya's edge.
Gaggan Anand inside the maison itself — dinner as a one-off collaboration between chef and house.
A research kitchen recovering lost Thai recipes, one seasonal menu at a time.
Grand riverside French dining in the Oriental's most storied room.
One of the world's defining modern-Thai kitchens, exacting and unafraid of real heat.
Antique Thai recipes, painstakingly researched and plated with a jeweller's care.
Regional Thai home cooking, gently refined — comfort with a Michelin star.
Old Thai cookbooks brought back to the table by chef David Thompson.
A teak-house kitchen guarding the grand old recipes of Thai gastronomy.
Bangkok's most sought-after sushi counter — Tokyo-grade omakase, near-impossible to book.
Swiss-French haute cuisine in a converted mansion, plated with quiet rigour.
A young couple's inventive, ingredient-driven cooking that keeps its star with ease.
Zero-waste, neo-Indian cooking grown in the restaurant's own urban farm.
Regional Indian cooking with a modern hand, and a rare Bangkok star for the cuisine.
The Ducasse standard on the river — classical French precision with a Bangkok view.
Andreas Caminada's shared-plate fine dining — generous, playful, refined.
French–Japanese cooking with skyline views from the Okura tower.
A refined French-leaning kitchen that quietly holds its star year on year.
Family Thai recipes served in a heritage shophouse, warm and unhurried.
Refined regional Thai cooking with a riverside sensibility.
A modern, boundary-pushing kitchen newly welcomed into the Michelin fold.
An inventive new one-star doing quiet, considered tasting menus.
A characterful newcomer that charmed the inspectors into a first star.
Thai ingredients, modern technique and a young, restless kitchen in old Chinatown.
The goggle-wearing grandmother who cooks her crab omelette over charcoal — and holds a Michelin star for it.
Bangkok's most famous pad thai, wrapped in a thin egg skin since 1966.
Central-Thai home cooking beloved by locals — the crab-and-yellow-chilli stir-fry is legend.
Urban-rustic Thai drinking food and grilled snacks from the Bo.lan team, by the river.
Phuketian Southern-Thai cooking — the famous crab curry and turmeric-rich dishes.
A no-frills lunchroom serving proper old-Bangkok curries to office crowds since the 1960s.
Comforting family-recipe Thai cooking, the kind grandmothers guard.
Crisp fried chicken buried under fried garlic — a Bangkok lunch pilgrimage.

venues.n: The Grand Palace & Wat Phra Kaew (Temple of the Emerald Buddha)
venues.d: Bangkok's single most important sight: the walled royal city of the Chakri kings, its glittering spires and murals surrounding the tiny, revered Emerald Buddha. Go at opening (8:30am) to beat the heat and coach crowds; a licensed private guide turns a crowded shuffle into a genuinely legible morning, and there is a strict cover-shoulders-and-knees dress code for the whole family.

venues.n: Wat Pho (Temple of the Reclining Buddha)
venues.d: A short walk south of the Grand Palace, home to the 46-metre gold-leaf Reclining Buddha and the birthplace of traditional Thai massage. End the visit with a proper hour-long massage at the on-site school for a fraction of a spa price. Open daily to 6:30pm, calmer in late afternoon.

The porcelain-encrusted Khmer-style prang rising from the west bank, best reached by the two-minute cross-river ferry from Tha Tien pier. Climb the steep steps for river views, then time your visit for golden hour when the spire glows; the reverse view from a Tha Tien rooftop bar at sunset is the classic photograph.

A gentle spiral of about 320 steps winds up Bangkok's only hill, past bells and prayer flags to a gold chedi and a 360-degree panorama over the Old Town rooftops. One of the finest free sunset perches in the city and refreshingly uncrowded.

venues.n: Wat Traimit (Temple of the Golden Buddha)
venues.d: Houses a 5.5-tonne solid-gold Buddha, over three metres tall, hidden under plaster for centuries and revealed by accident. Sits at the gateway to Chinatown, so pair it with a Yaowarat food crawl. The upstairs galleries tell the story of the Chinese community in Bangkok.

Built of white Carrara marble imported from Italy, this is the temple on the back of the old five-baht coin and one of Bangkok's most photogenic yet least crowded. The cloister of 52 Buddha images in different regional styles is a quiet, serene stop away from the tourist trail.

venues.n: Wat Ratchanatdaram & Loha Prasat (The Metal Castle)
venues.d: A 37-spired iron 'metal castle', the only structure of its kind still standing, its tapering black spires unlike anything else in Bangkok. Climb the spiral staircase past meditation cloisters to a top-level walkway with views to the Golden Mount and Democracy Monument.

The teak compound of the American 'Silk King' who revived the Thai silk trade then vanished in 1967, assembled from six antique houses and filled with Southeast Asian art. A garden oasis minutes from the shopping malls, with excellent guided tours, a serene café and a shop of genuinely good silk for gifts.

A private five-floor, 20,000-square-metre museum holding one of Thailand's finest collections of modern and contemporary Thai art, anchored by the works Thawan Duchanee. Air-conditioned, spacious and unhurried, it is an easy afternoon and a genuine highlight for art-minded travellers.

Southeast Asia's largest museum, set in a former palace, spanning Thai history from prehistory through the Sukhothai and Ayutthaya kingdoms, including the royal funeral chariots. Free English-language volunteer guided tours a few mornings a week are the best way to make sense of it before the temples.

A cluster of eight antique teak houses assembled by a prince and princess into a serene garden museum, its jewel the lacquer-and-gold Ban Chiang Lacquer Pavilion. Rarely busy, it is a graceful, discreet stop for those who found Jim Thompson's crowds too much.

The historic royal island threaded by canals, where the palaces, temples and old shophouses of Bangkok's founding cluster within walking distance. Wander from the Grand Palace past amulet markets, the giant swing at Wat Suthat and Sao Ching Cha, ideally early morning before the heat, on foot or by tuk-tuk.

Bangkok's most electric street-food strip: after sunset the neon comes on and woks roar along Yaowarat Road and its side lanes. Come hungry for seafood, dim sum, bird's-nest and mango sticky rice, and duck into the gold shops and old Chinese shrines. A guided evening food walk cuts through the chaos and can be tailored for vegetarian and Jain diners.

One of Bangkok's oldest quarters, a maze of Chinese shophouses, car-part workshops, hidden shrines, street art and hip cafés that rewards slow wandering by foot or bicycle. The riverside lanes here are genuinely atmospheric and refreshingly untouristed compared with Yaowarat.

venues.n: Charoen Krung & Bang Rak creative district
venues.d: Bangkok's first paved street, now the city's creative heart, where legendary street stalls sit beside boundary-pushing restaurants, galleries and the Warehouse 30 and TCDC design hubs. A good half-day of gallery-hopping, riverside cafés and boutique shopping for design-minded travellers.

Where affluent young Bangkok goes out: sleek wine bars, speakeasies, live-music rooms, top Japanese restaurants and upscale community malls like The Commons. The most polished, discreet nightlife in the city and a natural base for travellers staying in the modern Sukhumvit hotels.

A leafy, low-rise neighbourhood of independent cafés, small design shops and easygoing restaurants that feels like a village inside the megacity. Best explored on a slow morning of coffee-hopping, and blessedly quiet compared with Sukhumvit.

One of the world's largest markets: some 15,000 stalls across 35 acres of clothing, antiques, art, ceramics, plants and a serious food scene. Go early on a Saturday or Sunday to beat the heat, note the numbered sections so you can find your way back, and treat it as the city's great treasure hunt.

venues.n: Chao Phraya river & the express boat
venues.d: The river is Bangkok's original highway and the best way to link the big riverside sights. Hop the tourist or local express boat between Sathorn, the Old Town temples and ICONSIAM for a breezy, cheap, ever-changing view of barges, temples and skyscrapers. A private long-tail charter gives a family the same views on its own schedule.

Slip off the main river into the quiet canals of Thonburi, past stilt houses, orchid gardens, riverside temples and the giant Buddha of Wat Paknam. The classic 'Venice of the East' experience; a private long-tail lets you set the pace and stop at the Artist's House (Baan Silapin) for coffee and a puppet show.

A two-hour glide past the floodlit Grand Palace, Wat Arun and the bridges, with Thai and international dinner service on board. The premium cruises are a genuinely lovely, low-effort evening for multi-generational groups; book a window or open-deck table and confirm vegetarian menus in advance.

Bangkok's highest public viewpoint on the 78th floor of King Power Mahanakhon (about 314 metres), including a glass-floor tray for the brave and an open rooftop bar. The clearest, most modern panorama of the whole city, best at dusk as the lights come on.

The golden-domed rooftop bar made famous by 'The Hangover Part II', perched 63 floors above the Chao Phraya with an unmatched sweep of the river bend. A smart-casual dress code applies and cocktails are premium-priced; come for the view and the occasion rather than the value.

An open-air rooftop restaurant and bar on the 61st floor with a 360-degree horizon and no glass to spoil the view. The most romantic of the sky bars for a couple; book a railing table a few days ahead for sunset.

Bangkok's first and best-loved park, a green lung of lakes, jogging paths, banyan trees and resident monitor lizards in the heart of the business district. Come at dawn for the tai chi and free open-air aerobics, or rent a pedal boat with the children in the late afternoon.

A striking rewilded wetland park with elevated walkways over lotus ponds and reed beds, so lush that rare birds have returned to the city. Linked to Lumpini by the elevated 'Green Mile' skywalk, it is a superb early-morning walk or run right next to the Sukhumvit hotels.

An artificial-island loop of jungle, mangrove and canal just across the river, laced with raised concrete cycle paths through backyard gardens. Rent a bicycle, visit the floating Bang Nam Phueng weekend market and Sri Nakhon Khuean Khan Park; the closest thing to countryside within reach of downtown.

A 69-metre seated Buddha towers over the canals, but the real wonder is the fifth-floor emerald glass stupa beneath a cosmic ceiling mural that has made this one of Bangkok's most photographed temples. Still set in a genuinely local canal-side neighbourhood, it pairs naturally with a Thonburi boat tour.

A colossal three-headed bronze elephant crowns a museum whose interior is an extravagant journey from an underworld basement up through an earthly floor to a heaven of stained glass and a spiral staircase. The eccentric vision of collector Lek Viriyaphant; a memorable, unusual stop for families en route to the Ancient City.

An enormous open-air park shaped like Thailand, dotted with over 100 scaled replicas and restorations of the country's greatest monuments. Rent a golf cart or bicycle and cover the whole kingdom in an afternoon; a clever, uncrowded outing with older children who found the city temples tiring.

A vast riverside luxury mall with global flagships, a landmark waterfront and the indoor SookSiam floating-market food hall recreating all 77 provinces under one roof. The nightly musical fountain show on the river is free; a good rainy-afternoon or air-conditioned family stop with genuinely broad dining, including easy vegetarian options.

A converted riverside warehouse district of shops, restaurants and a big Ferris wheel, reached by a free shuttle boat from Sathorn pier as the sun sets over the water. An easy, relaxed evening for families, with the option of a ladyboy cabaret or Muay Thai Live show on site.

Bangkok's buzziest night market of the moment, over 1,500 white-tent stalls of street food, drinks and clothing beside the MRT, famous for the leaning-tower 'volcano' pork ribs. Come hungry after 6pm; lively, young and easy to reach by metro.

venues.n: Talad Rot Fai (Train Night Market), Srinakarin
venues.d: A sprawling vintage-and-antiques night market of retro cars, warehouse bars, collectibles and food, best seen from the overlooking rooftop bars where the rows of tents glow at night. More characterful and less polished than the mall night markets, open Thursday to Sunday evenings.

The world's first purpose-built Muay Thai stadium, where an evening card opens with the ritual wai kru dance to live music. The most storied, authentic place to see Thailand's national sport; ringside seats put you in the thick of it, and it is a genuine spectacle for a first-timer.

venues.n: Khon masked dance at Sala Chalermkrung
venues.d: The centuries-old royal masked dance-drama, retelling the Ramakien (Thai Ramayana) with ornate costumes and precise gesture, staged in a landmark 1933 theatre. A refined, unmistakably Thai evening of culture; the Ramayana story is familiar and resonant for Indian visitors.

Bangkok's best-known ladyboy cabaret, a glossy hour of song, dance and impersonation of global icons. Light, fun and family-workable as an evening's entertainment, easily combined with dinner and a stroll at Asiatique.

The best classes start with a guided market tour to choose lemongrass, galangal and chillies, then walk you through a green curry, tom yum and mango sticky rice you eat together. A hands-on half-day the whole family enjoys; most schools happily run fully vegetarian or Jain-friendly menus if asked ahead.

venues.n: Traditional Thai massage at Wat Pho
venues.d: Take your massage where the art is taught: the school inside Wat Pho is the recognised home of traditional Thai massage, and an hour here is authentic, superb value and part of the temple visit itself. The gentle starting point before the grander spas.

A garden-villa spa group that has become Bangkok's benchmark for the luxury Thai spa experience, with long signature aromatherapy rituals in private, tranquil rooms. Ideal for a couple's afternoon or an unhurried treat; book a signature package ahead as it is deservedly popular.
Bangkok's original jazz bar since 1953, in the grande dame of the river — the city's most storied room for a drink.
The bar the region rates above all others in Bangkok right now — precise, personal, and quietly brilliant.
The city's most talked-about newcomer — a studio-like counter that vaulted straight into the region's top five.
A golden-age Buenos Aires grand café on the river, inside the Four Seasons — glamour done with real substance.
A run-down-cathedral cocktail temple on Chinatown's edgiest lane — creative, theatrical, open late.
Silom's most serious cocktail room, holding its own since 2014 with an aperitivo sensibility and quiet mastery.
A speakeasy over the top floors of a 120-year-old shophouse that was once an opium den — drinks with a Chinatown soul.

venues.n: Bar Sathorn, The House on Sathorn
venues.d: Modern mixology inside an 1889 mansion that has been a merchant's home, a hotel and an embassy — history in a glass.
A Thai-ingredient-led bar that has ranked among Asia's very best — refined, seasonal, deeply of this place.

venues.n: Sky Bar, lebua at State Tower
venues.d: The open-air perch 63 floors up that the world knows from film — the definitive Bangkok skyline drink.
An open-edge deck on the 61st floor with nothing between you and the whole of Bangkok.
A vivid rooftop 76 floors up in the city's most striking tower — the highest of Bangkok's serious sky bars.
